description: The main goal of ድንቅነሽ team is to create a community of scientists that are interested in strengthening space science sector in developing countries such as Ethiopia. In the upcoming NASA space app challenge hosted in Addis Ababa,  we are taking on the challenge 'Abandoned but not forgotten: Space Equipment on Mars and the Moon with the help of my teammates. I'm looking for teammates with skills in HTML, CSS, JavaScript, or video editing.
summary: We chose the  topic called "Abandoned but not forgotten: storytelling about NASA's discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars." Instead of relying on plain text to narrate NASA's missions, we developed a platform that engages audiences of all ages through storytelling. Our website is divided into two main sections: one designed for children under 13 and another tailored for users aged 13 and above. The former section is built for children under 13 with exciting animations, including an avatar called Lucy, that helps them navigate through the websites and keeps them engaged. Basically, Lucy, the squirrel, is an avatar that leads the kids through the website by launching herself to mars or to the moon. The section made for people above 13 has a full history of the equipment mentioned and has an engaging 3D model of each equipment when it was launched. In each of the section, we classified the missions to two: lunar and martial missions. In Lunar missions, we mentioned Apollo 11 descendant stage, and Apollo 15 lunar module while in Martian missions, we talked about Viking 1 Lander, Ingenuity Helicopter and Spirit and Opportunity rovers. We clearly stated what their roles were in revolutionizing Space Science and that they were the milestones of the innovation of advanced satellites and vehicles that are successfully executing their mission on the Moon and Mars.
details:
ድንቅነሽ (Dinkinesh) Space Museum — Abandoned but not Forgotten is an interactive 3D web museum built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to tell the stories of NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars. Because no one can walk up to a lander or rover on another world, these historic machines are often forgotten inside flat textbook photos and long timelines. Our project brings them within reach in any modern web browser through interactive 3D exploration and storytelling.
Visitors start by choosing a world—the Moon or Mars—then orbit, zoom, and explore each machine’s story. To serve different ages effectively, the project features two tailored web experiences. The Kids’ Edition is led by Lucy the squirrel astronaut, who launches in her spacecraft to proportional 3D globes of the Moon and Mars. Young explorers tap landing sites—including Apollo 11, Apollo 15, Viking 1, Spirit and Opportunity, and Ingenuity—to read short, clear stories and test what they learned in Lucy’s Space Quiz. The 3D Museum (Adults’ Edition) offers an atmospheric deep-space exhibition where visitors inspect authentic 3D spacecraft models, including the Sojourner rover, alongside mission dates, goals, landing sites, and outcomes.
The key benefit of Dinkinesh Museum is instant, accessible learning: anyone with a phone or computer browser can explore real planetary hardware with zero downloads or VR headsets required. Our intended impact is to spark curiosity in students under 13 and space enthusiasts of any age, while providing a scalable framework for classroom use that can expand to additional NASA missions, component hotspots, and languages such as Amharic.
Developed on standard laptops and tested across desktop and mobile devices, the project is built with TypeScript, React, Tailwind CSS, Vite, and Three.js for real-time WebGL 3D rendering, managed on GitHub and deployed via Netlify. Every exhibit is powered by NASA Open Data, pairing .glb 3D spacecraft and planetary models from NASA 3D Resources with verified mission histories from science.nasa.gov.
Creatively, the museum unites Ethiopian heritage and space exploration through its name: ድንቅነሽ (Dinkinesh) means “You are wonderful” in Amharic and is the Ethiopian name of the fossil Lucy, inspiring our children’s guide. Throughout development, our team balanced contrasting visual tones—playful warmth for children and dark archival focus for adults—alongside proportional distances between real landing sites, fast .glb model loading across everyday internet connections, and a clean click-to-explore interface that works effortlessly on any screen.
